abajo.note: In an address, abajo means west - where the sun goes down

acuerdo.note: Agree the fare before you get in. Always

ahorita.note: Not a length of time. It states an intention, and the tone tells you which

albergar.note: 'Albergar una esperanza' = to harbor a hope

albur.note: A pun with a hidden, often cheeky, second meaning

almuerzo.note: At twelve, and the big meal of the day

amanecer.en: to stay up till dawn / dawn

amar.note: Bigger than querer, and used far less. Many never say it

amañarse.note: To grow attached to a place

amor.note: 'Mi amor' is said to almost anybody, warmly

apoyar.note: Emotional support; 'te apoyo' = I support you

argumento.note: A point you make, not a fight

arriba.note: In an address, arriba means east - where the sun comes up

asimismo.note: Elegant way to add a point

aspirar.note: In Nica speech, the 's' is aspirated or dropped

bicho.note: Informal — a bug, or affectionately a kid

bolsa.note: Water and juice are sold in bags here, not bottles

buena onda.note: 'Es buena onda' = he's a cool/kind person

buenas.note: Short for buenos días/buenas tardes. The everyday Nica greeting

cae bien.note: 'Me cae bien' = I like him/her (as a person)

cafecito.note: Diminutive of café — warmth, not size

calmarse.note: Telling somebody to is pouring petrol on it

calor.note: 'Hace calor' = it's hot. 'Tengo calor' = I'm hot

camión.note: In Mexico = bus; in Nicaragua a bus is 'bus'

captar.note: To catch a meaning or hint

carcajada.note: 'Soltar la carcajada' = to burst out laughing

chele.note: Nica slang. Not offensive. Fem: chela

chinear.en: to carry and fuss over a child
chinear.note: More than carrying. Carrying with affection

chunche.note: Any object whose name you do not know. Gets you out of anything

ciento.note: Used in compound numbers: ciento treinta = 130

comedor.note: A house with tables. You point at the pots

comprender.note: A touch more formal than entender

conceder.note: In debate, to grant a point

cuadra.note: Distances here are counted in cuadras, corner to corner

córdoba.note: The currency. Written córdoba, said peso

delicado.note: Nobody says grave out loud. Saying it seems like calling it

disculpa.note: Three parts: what you did, that it was your fault, what you will do

doble sentido.note: A phrase with a hidden, often cheeky, second meaning

dominar.note: 'Dominar un idioma' = to master a language

encantar.note: Stronger than gustar. 'Me encanta' = I love it

fiado.note: Buying now, paying later — common at pulperías

formulario.note: A paper form to fill out

fritanga.note: Sets up at dusk. You eat standing in the street

fíjate.note: 'Fíjate que...' = a classic way to start telling news

gallopinto.note: Nica national dish: rice and beans fried together

gordo.note: Not an insult here. Also used as an endearment

gustar.note: Me gusta = I like (it pleases me)

hogar.note: Home as a feeling, warmer than 'casa'

ideay.note: Uniquely Nicaraguan. Means whatever the tone means

invierno.note: Means the rains, not cold. It is hot all year

jaña.note: Casual Nica slang for a girl or girlfriend

jodido.note: 'Qué jodido' - what a pain. Very common, mildly coarse

lago.note: 'Al lago' means north - the lake is north of Managua

maje.note: Like 'dude' — affectionate among friends, rude with strangers

mandado.note: Being sent on one means you belong to the house

mantener.note: 'Mantener mi punto' = to hold my point

moraleja.note: The lesson of a story or fable

mujer.note: 'Mi mujer' is the ordinary word here and carries none of the English weight

nacatamal.note: Sunday food. Bought early or it is gone

ojalá.note: Heard constantly. Everything you want and do not control

oído.note: The trained ear for understanding speech

parada.note: Often just a corner with people waiting

pega.note: 'Echarse un pega' = take a short nap

perdonar.note: Apologise once. Repeating it loads it back on them

pillar.note: To catch on to a joke or meaning

pinche.note: In Nica: stingy or low-quality (milder than Mexican usage)

pinolero.note: From pinol, from maize. What Nicaraguans call themselves

platica.note: 'Platicar' = to chat. Common in Central America

platicar.note: Common in Central America for casual talk

por ende.note: Formal connector, more refined than 'por eso'

puente.note: Often figurative: a bridge between worlds

pulpería.note: Somebody's front room with a grille. Sells anything, in any quantity

quizás.note: Often a soft 'no' in social contexts

reclamo.note: 'Hacer un reclamo' = to make a complaint

refresco.note: Water with fruit, not a fizzy drink. Always sweet

refrán.note: A traditional fixed saying — beloved in daily speech

regatear.note: Clothes and taxis yes. Food, buses and the pulpería never

registro.note: Formal vs informal level of language

relajo.note: 'Echar relajo' = to goof around, have fun

retruécano.note: A clever reversal of words for effect

saludar.note: Not greeting somebody you pass is the rudest thing you can do

sano.note: Humor that's 'sano' is good-natured, not crude

saudade.note: A bittersweet longing — borrowed feeling, deeply felt

suegra.note: Usted forever, even after she calls you mijo

vacilar.note: Done to the people you like. Being spared it means you are still a guest

vigorón.en: yuca, chicharrón and curtido on a leaf

vos.note: Nica uses vos not tú. Changes conjugations

voseo.note: The vos pronoun system, universal in Nicaragua

árbol.note: Trees that were cut down decades ago are still used as addresses

abril.note: The hottest month in Nicaragua, at the end of the dry season

acertar.en: to get it right, to land it

achiote.note: The red seed paste that colours Nicaraguan meat

acomodado.note: What you say instead of rico, which sounds like a complaint

acostarse.en: to lie down/to go to bed

acá.note: Nicaragua says acá at least as often as aquí

adoptivo.note: Nica adoptivo - said about you, never to you

agrio.note: Naranja agria - sour orange, used the way lemon is elsewhere

aguante.note: What the priest talks about at a wedding, more than love

ah.note: Recognition, not surprise. 'Áh, sí' = oh, right

ahoritita.note: Ahorita with another -ita. It can still mean in an hour

aire.note: 'No tiene aire' about a car means no air conditioning

ajeno.note: Sentirse ajeno - to feel you are from elsewhere

alegría.note: '¿Quién causa tanta alegría?' - the Gritería call

alfombra.note: In Semana Santa, a carpet of dyed sawdust laid in the street for the procession to walk over

alguno.note: Shortens to algún before a masculine noun

altar.note: Built in the front room for La Purísima

amorcito.note: Amor with -ito on it. Nicaragua puts -ito on everything

antemano.note: Only ever met in de antemano = in advance

antorcha.note: Run from Guatemala hand to hand, arriving for the fifteenth

aparte.note: Aparte de eso = apart from that

apellido.note: You have two: father's first, mother's second

apodo.note: Everybody has one. You do not choose it

aprovechar.en: to take advantage of, to make use of
aprovechar.note: Aprovechando que estamos aqui - the softest way into a request

arrecho.note: Both, and the tone decides. Never with elders, never in front of a lady

así.note: Así es = that is how it is

atrasarse.en: to be late, to fall behind

aun.note: Aun así = even so. With an accent, aún means still

autonomía.note: The Caribbean regions have had their own government since 1987

ayudante.note: Shouts the route, takes the fare, never sits down

baho.note: Meat, plantain and yuca steamed in layers under plantain leaves. A house dish, never a restaurant one

bajito.note: Hablar bajito = to talk under your breath

bendición.note: Children ask elders for it as a greeting. 'Bendición' - 'Dios te bendiga'

bomba.note: A shouted rhyme at a party - somebody yells ¡Bomba! and everyone stops to hear it

borracho.note: A sad drunk is pitied, a fighting drunk loses his friends

brindar.note: Touch every bottle, and look them in the face

brindis.en: the little gift handed out at a Purisima door
brindis.note: Caps, limes, cajeta, sweets - a household saves for it all year

bulla.note: Not a nuisance here, the weather. A quiet block on a Saturday means something happened

cachimbo.note: Stronger than monton. Among friends, not with the suegra

caponera.note: What people actually call it. Mototaxi is the paperwork word

caso.note: 'Hacer caso' - to do as you are told

celos.note: Not strange here. Denying them is what is strange

certeza.note: Speaking with certeza about everything sounds boastful here

chancho.note: Nicaragua says chancho, not cerdo, for the live animal

chavalito.note: Chavalo is a kid; chavalito is a small one

chela.note: Nicaraguan slang. A chele is a fair-skinned person - same word, different job

chico.note: Also a kid. Chiquito is the everyday word here

chischil.note: The Purisima gift children fight over and mothers hate

chisme.note: The newspaper of the barrio, and it changes at every mouth

chismosa.note: Not a serious insult - a good one is useful

citar.note: A dead grandmother cannot be argued with. That is what makes the quote work

coco.note: Cooking with coco is Caribbean-coast, not Managua

colorado.note: Ponerse colorado = to go red in the face

compadrazgo.note: The bond between parents and godparents - family without blood

compadre.note: A family you choose. More than a friend, and it does not end

componer.note: Nicaragua mends things. Buying a new one is odd

conseguir.note: Aquí no se consigue = you cannot get it here

conservador.note: One of the two old parties - Granada was conservative, León liberal

contradecir.note: Not forbidden - forbidden in front of other people

convenir.note: No me conviene = it is not worth it for me

conversar.note: Nicaragua says conversar. Platicar is Mexican

copia.note: Bring two of everything. Nobody will tell you which

copla.note: What the Enano Cabezon shouts at your door in December

costeño.note: Half the country, and a different set of languages

criollo.note: The English-based language of Bluefields - not Spanish

cualquiera.note: Shortens to cualquier in front of a noun

cuanto.note: En cuanto = as soon as. Cuanto antes = as soon as possible

cuarentena.en: the forty days after a birth
cuarentena.note: She does nothing. Her mother moves in

cuarta.note: Cuarto is a room, so the number keeps its own entry

cumbia.note: The first thing they put on. The step is in the hips

defenderse.en: to get by/to hold your own
defenderse.note: The verb used for coping here, as if living were something you stand up to

departamento.note: Nicaragua's provinces. Small enough to cross three in a morning

devoto.note: Somebody paying a promise to a saint with their body

diminutivo.note: Does not shrink the thing. It brings it closer

dios.note: Si Dios quiere - said about anything in the future

dirección.note: An address here is landmarks, not a street and number

disimular.en: to cover up, to not let it show

doler.note: The pain happens to you: 'me duele la cabeza', not 'I have a headache'

educación.note: 'Mala educación' means bad manners, not bad schooling

embargo.note: Only ever met in sin embargo = however

enano.note: El Enano Cabezon - the big-headed boy who recites beside the Gigantona

encargar.en: to order, to ask somebody to bring
encargar.note: You encargar from a neighbour, not from a business

enganchar.note: How you interrupt without offending: repeat his last two words

entendedor.note: A buen entendedor, pocas palabras - a word to the wise

exagerar.note: Not lying - a story is expected to grow in the telling

fama.note: Every barrio has one, and it is put there by people who never went in

fiar.note: Doña Chepa's notebook holds half the street

fijarse.note: 'Fíjese que' warns you a no is coming

fin.note: Por fin = at last. Fin de semana = weekend

fulano.note: Fulano, mengano y zutano - Spanish for Tom, Dick and Harry

gallo pinto.note: The national breakfast. Eaten most mornings of most lives

gas.note: La cocina de gas - the bottled gas most kitchens run on

gigantona.note: The three-metre dancing doll of the December streets, strongest in Leon

gracia.note: Tener gracia is to be funny, not to be graceful

gringo.note: Not an insult here on its own - it just means a North American

gritería.note: December 7. The whole country goes door to door shouting the answer

haber.note: Never on its own: he comido, había llegado. Hay is its own word

hallarse.en: to feel at home in a place
hallarse.note: No me hallo - you do not fit here, and nobody asks you to explain why

hoja.note: A plantain leaf is the plate at a fritanga

igualito.note: Igual with -ito on it: igualito a su papá

imagen.note: Not a photograph - the wooden figure of a saint carried in a procession

imperfecto.note: Also the past tense for what used to happen: yo hablaba

interlocal.note: Leaves when it is full, not at a time

jaja.note: Written laughter. The j is an h sound

jerarquía.note: The written one and the real one. Age and time inside outrank a job title

letanía.note: The sung part of the Purisima, after the shouted question

liberal.note: The other old party. The rivalry is two centuries old

luz.note: 'Se fue la luz' - the power went. Said with no drama at all

mapa.note: Of limited use in a city with no street names

materno.note: The second surname. Everybody here has two

medio.note: Medio día = half a day. Media hora = half an hour

medir.note: Medir es de gente que no sabe - a cook with sazon measures nothing

mijo.note: From 'mi hijo'. Warmth, not literal. Being called it means something

modo.note: Ni modo = nothing to be done about it

motivo.note: A delay with a motivo is only a delay. Without one it is disrespect

muletilla.note: pues, va, fijate, ideay - what holds a conversation up

muñeco.note: The ano viejo muneco sits on the pavement and burns at midnight

mí.note: Only after a preposition: para mí, a mí, de mí

neblina.note: It comes down at four in Jinotega and gets under the door

ninguno.note: Shortens to ningún before a masculine noun

nomás.note: Nicaraguan to the bone: pase nomás, aquí nomás

novena.note: Nine nights of prayer after a death, or before a saint's day

ofensa.note: Not the same as a hurt - an ofensa is public and it keeps

oler.note: Huele a café. The stem changes: huelo, olés, huele

oír.note: Oigo, oís, oye. Escuchar is to listen on purpose

padrino.note: Each pays for one thing. That is how a wedding happens without money

panga.note: How you finish the journey to Bluefields

panza.note: Understanding a joke with the panza and not the head is the last thing to arrive

parejo.note: Parejo is Nicaraguan for evenly - hervir parejo

patio.note: Often has no wall. The neighbours' patio is the same patio

patria.note: September is 'el mes de la patria'

pausa.note: A pause before the word bien means he is not fine, and nobody will ask further

pescao.note: Coast pronunciation of pescado - the d drops on the Caribbean side

peso.note: What everyone actually calls a córdoba out loud

pila.note: Cement tank kept full. You never get in it - you scoop from it

pinolillo.note: The national drink. Stir it or you drink sweet water

pista.note: Two chairs moved aside is already a pista

portón.note: Where the real goodbye happens - the only place with no witnesses

prisa.note: 'Tengo prisa' - I am in a hurry. Rarely useful here

puchica.note: The polite version of a swear word. Central America's own

purísima.note: The 7th of December. Doors open, everyone sings, and the house gives out sweets

pésame.note: 'Mi pésame' and a handshake. Not that she is in a better place

pítcher.note: Baseball is the national sport, and the words came with it

pólvora.note: Nicaraguan polvora is about noise, not light

queque.note: Nicaragua says queque, from the English

quesillo.en: cheese in a tortilla with cream and onion

quinceañera.en: a girl turning fifteen, and her party

quincena.note: The 15th and the 30th. The whole city changes on those days

rarísimo.note: -ísimo is how you say very: rarísimo, buenísimo, rapidísimo

recarga.note: Bought at any pulpería, by phone number

recomendar.note: Worth more than a CV. Whoever recommends you answers for you

relación.note: What an excuse is protecting. The job stays just as late

remesa.note: Money from a relative abroad. Half the street lives on it

rincón.note: Esquina is a street corner, rincon is an indoor one

riquísimo.note: Rico with -ísimo on it - the everyday word for good food

robar.note: 'Me robaron' - it was stolen from me, never 'I lost it'

rondón.note: Caribbean coast stew: fish, yuca, plantain and coconut milk

ruta.note: Managua buses are rutas, by number. Never 'camión'

sazón.en: the hand of the person cooking
sazón.note: Not the recipe and not the ingredients. Two women with the same pot do not get the same thing

serenata.note: Sung to mothers at midnight on the twenty-ninth of May

seño.note: How you address a woman behind a counter

soler.note: Suele llegar tarde = he usually arrives late

solicitar.note: On paper you say solicito, unsoftened. In speech you would never

sonar.note: Stem-changing: suena. Used constantly about how a word lands

suavizar.note: The imperfect does it: queria preguntarle, not quiero

tanda.note: Ordered for the whole table, never for yourself

tanque.note: The water tank on the roof, filled when the water comes

tercero.note: Shortens to 'tercer' before a masculine noun

terremoto.note: The 1972 earthquake flattened central Managua. The addresses outlived the buildings

tiburón.note: Lake Cocibolca had freshwater sharks. The old people still talk about them

tocar.note: 'Me toca' - it is my turn. Being whose turn it is means you are inside

tocayo.note: Not a coincidence here - a relationship. Two tocayos use the word instead of the name

tope.note: Managua, August 1: Santo Domingo comes down from Las Sierritas into the city

tortilla.note: Thick maize tortilla, not the thin Mexican kind

tutear.note: In Nicaragua tutear sounds foreign - it is vos or usted

tú.note: The form Nicaragua does not use. It is vos here, or usted

ustedes.note: There is no vosotros anywhere in Latin America

uva.note: Twelve at midnight, one wish with each

uy.note: The noise for surprise or a small fright

vacilón.note: From vacilar. Teasing done as affection - the one nobody vacila is the one nobody knows

vaho.note: Beef, yuca and plantain steamed in banana leaves - a Sunday dish

valer.note: Vale la pena = it is worth the trouble

vals.note: Danced with the father first, at the quince

vara.note: Ni de vara - not a chance, and not up for discussion

varilla.note: Left standing out of the roof on purpose. It means there will be a second floor one day

velorio.note: You go, even if you did not know them

ventilador.note: Nicaragua says abanico for the ceiling kind

volumen.note: Shouting means it still matters. Cold politeness is what is serious

voz.note: 'Nota de voz' - a voice note, how people actually talk

patterns.title: Voseo — The Nica 'You'
patterns.text:
Nicaragua uses 'vos' instead of 'tú'. This changes conjugations:

• Tú tienes → Vos tenés
• Tú quieres → Vos querés
• Tú sabes → Vos sabés

Pattern: stress the last syllable, drop -ie- stems.

Commands: stress final syllable:
• Mira → Mirá • Anda → Andá • Toma → Tomá

You'll never hear 'tú' in Nicaragua.

patterns.title: Ser vs Estar — Two 'Be' Verbs
patterns.text:
SER — permanent things:
• Soy de EEUU (origin)
• Es doctora (profession)
• Es grande (inherent quality)

ESTAR — temporary/location:
• Estoy en Managua (location)
• Estoy enfermo (temp state)
• Está bueno (right now)

If it can change → estar.
If it defines what something IS → ser.

patterns.title: Me gusta — Backwards 'Liking'
patterns.text:
English: 'I like the food'
Spanish: 'Me gusta la comida' (food pleases me)

Subject is FLIPPED:
• Me gusta el arroz (I like rice)
• Me gustan los mangos (I like mangos)
• ¿Te gusta Nicaragua?

Gusta = one thing. Gustan = multiple things.

patterns.title: Nica Directions — No Street Names
patterns.text:
Managua has no street names. Everything is landmarks + compass:

• '2 cuadras al norte del parque'
• Arriba = east (sun comes up)
• Abajo = west (sun goes down)
• Al lago = toward Lake Managua

'De la Rotonda, 3 arriba, 1 al sur, casa esquinera.'

patterns.title: Tener Expressions — 'To Have' = 'To Be'
patterns.text:
Spanish uses 'tener' (to have) where English uses 'to be':

• Tengo hambre = I'm hungry (I have hunger)
• Tengo 25 años = I'm 25 (I have 25 years)
• Tengo miedo = I'm scared (I have fear)
• Tiene razón = He's right (He has reason)
• Tengo sed = I'm thirsty (I have thirst)
• Tengo frío/calor = I'm cold/hot

patterns.title: Buenas — The Greeting You Always Use
patterns.text:
'Buenas' on its own works all day and with anybody.

• Buenas (morning, noon or night)
• Buenos días until about eleven
• Buenas tardes, buenas noches

You greet BEFORE you ask for anything. Walking into a pulpería and saying what you want is what badly brought up people do.

Passing somebody on the pavement? Buenas. That is the whole exchange.

patterns.title: Usted or Vos — Who Gets Which
patterns.text:
Two ways of saying 'you', and picking wrong is louder than a mistake.

VOS — friends, workmates, anybody your own age, children.
USTED — older people, a boss, a stranger, an official, a customer.

• Vos tenés / Usted tiene
• Vení / Venga
• ¿Cómo estás vos? / ¿Cómo está usted?

When in doubt use usted. Being too respectful costs nothing; being too familiar with a doña costs a lot.

The other person will drop you to vos when they are ready. Follow them.

patterns.title: -ito — Small, Soft, or Sooner
patterns.text:
The -ito ending does far more than 'small'.

• un ratito — a little while (softens a long wait)
• ahorita — from 'ahora', but vaguer, not sharper
• un cafecito — a coffee, offered warmly
• despacito — nice and slowly

It takes the edge off a request: 'Espereme un ratito' is gentler than 'Espere'.

Nicaraguans put it on almost anything. You will hear ahoritita — the diminutive of the diminutive.

patterns.title: Pesos, Reales, Córdobas
patterns.text:
The currency is the córdoba. Almost nobody says córdoba.

• 'Cien pesos' means a hundred córdobas
• 'reales' is money in general — ¿andás con reales?
• 'plata' is the everyday word for money

Prices are said fast and without the unit: 'Son cuarenta.'

Nobody asks what you earn. Money is talked around, never at: 'está difícil la cosa', 'ando corto', 'no alcanza'.

patterns.title: Hay — There Is, There Isn't
patterns.text:
'Hay' never changes. One form for singular and plural.

• Hay agua hoy — there is water today
• No hay luz — the power is out
• ¿Hay pan? — do you have bread?

Half of daily life here is a 'hay' question: hay agua, hay luz, hay pasaje, hay cupo.

'No hay' is a complete answer and you will get it a lot. It is not rudeness, it is a fact about the day.

patterns.title: Ando buscando — Andar Instead of Estar
patterns.text:
Nicaraguans use 'andar' where a textbook uses 'estar'.

• Ando buscando trabajo — I'm looking for work
• Anda enfermo — he's ill (at the moment)
• ¿Andás con plata? — have you got money on you?

Andar carries 'going about', so it fits an ongoing state better than estar does.

You will hear it constantly. Using it is one of the fastest ways to stop sounding like a course.

patterns.title: Voy a — The Future Nobody Bothers Conjugating
patterns.text:
The proper future tense exists. Almost nobody uses it in speech.

• Voy a comprar — I'm going to buy
• Vamos a ver — we'll see (and often: no)
• ¿Qué vas a hacer? — what are you going to do?

IR + A + infinitive covers nearly everything.

The real future turns up mostly in guesses: '¿Será?' — I wonder. 'Serán las tres' — it must be about three.

patterns.title: Regáleme — Give Me, Politely
patterns.text:
'Regalar' means to give as a present. In a shop it means something else entirely.

• Regáleme dos panes — could I have two rolls
• Regáleme un vaso de agua

Nobody thinks you are asking for a gift. It is simply the softest way to ask across a counter.

The scale, from blunt to soft:
• Deme dos — give me two
• Me da dos, por favor
• Regáleme dos

patterns.title: Question Words, Nica Order
patterns.text:
The words are ordinary. The habits are not.

• ¿Y vos qué? — and you? (asks for your opinion, seriously)
• ¿Qué te doy? — what can I get you (in a fritanga)
• ¿Para dónde? — where to (in a taxi)
• ¿Cuánto me cobra? — how much will you charge me

'¿Mande?' is Mexican. Here you say '¿Cómo?' or just '¿Ah?'

Note that price is asked as what you will be CHARGED, not what it costs.

patterns.title: Ayer — Talking About Yesterday
patterns.text:
The preterite is what happened and finished.

• -AR: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron
• -ER/-IR: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron

The ones you will actually need are irregular:
• fui (ser AND ir — same forms)
• tuve, estuve, hice, dije, vine

Note 'hablamos' is both present and preterite. Context decides, and nobody minds.

patterns.title: Cuando era chavalo — The Past That Was Ongoing
patterns.text:
The imperfect is what USED to happen, or was happening.

• -AR: hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablaban
• -ER/-IR: comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comían

Only three irregulars in the whole language: era, iba, veía.

• Cuando era chavalo jugaba en la calle
• Mi abuela cocinaba todos los domingos

Preterite = it happened. Imperfect = that is how things were.

patterns.title: Me levanto — Doing It To Yourself
patterns.text:
A pronoun in front turns the verb back on the doer.

• Me levanto a las cinco
• Se baña en la pila
• Sentate — sit yourself down

Some verbs change meaning entirely:
• ir = to go / irse = to leave
• quedar = to be left / quedarse = to stay
• acordar = to agree / acordarse = to remember

With vos commands the pronoun sticks on the end and the stress stays put: sentate, fijate, acordate.

patterns.title: Se lo — Two Pronouns in a Row
patterns.text:
When both pronouns turn up, the person comes first.

• Se lo doy — I'll give it to him
• Me lo dijo ayer — he told me it yesterday
• Te la traigo mañana — I'll bring it to you tomorrow

'Le lo' is never said. It becomes 'se lo'.

They stack onto an infinitive or a gerund:
• Voy a dárselo / Se lo voy a dar — both fine

patterns.title: Saber and Conocer — Two Kinds of Knowing
patterns.text:
SABER — facts, information, how to do something.
• Sé que viene el jueves
• ¿Sabés manejar?

CONOCER — being acquainted with a person or a place.
• ¿Conocés a Marcos?
• No conozco León

'Ya sé llegar' — I know how to get there.
'Ya conozco el barrio' — I know the barrio now.

In the preterite conocer means MET: 'La conocí en una fiesta.'

patterns.title: Por and Para
patterns.text:
PARA — where it is going, who it is for, what it is for.
• Para dónde va (destination)
• Es para mi mamá (recipient)
• Para el jueves (deadline)

POR — the reason, the route, the exchange.
• Gracias por venir (cause)
• Pasé por el mercado (through)
• Lo compré por cien (in exchange for)

Useful pair: 'trabajo para él' (I work for him, he is my boss) versus 'trabajo por él' (I am covering his shift).

patterns.title: Más que — Comparing Things
patterns.text:
• más ... que — more than
• menos ... que — less than
• tan ... como — as ... as

Four have their own word: mejor, peor, mayor, menor.

Nicaraguan comparisons are usually jokes:
• Sos más lento que un domingo
• Está más perdido que yo

Building one of those is how you answer being teased.

patterns.title: Bien caro — Saying How Much
patterns.text:
'Bien' is used where a textbook would use 'muy'.

• Está bien caro — it's really expensive
• Bien bueno, bien lejos, bien temprano

Stronger still:
• un montón — loads (safe with anybody)
• un cachimbo de — loads (friends only)
• -ísimo — rapidísimo, buenísimo

'Muy' is not wrong. It is just what a foreigner says.

patterns.title: Hablá, comé, vení — Vos Commands
patterns.text:
The vos command is the infinitive minus the -r, with the stress on the end.

• hablar → hablá
• comer → comé
• vivir → viví

There are almost no exceptions. Even the verbs that are irregular everywhere else behave: tener → tené, poner → poné, salir → salí.

Only 'ir' is odd: 'andá' is used instead.

With a pronoun attached the stress does not move: sentate, fijate, decime, acordate.

patterns.title: Fijate que no — Refusing Without a No
patterns.text:
Almost nobody here says a flat no. It leaves the person who asked looking bad.

What a no sounds like:
• Tal vez después — no
• Quizás — no
• Vamos a ver — no
• Ahorita está complicado — no, and it is not about you
• Si Dios quiere — no

THE SIGNAL IS THE DATE. Somebody who wants to come names a day. Somebody who says 'después' with no day has refused.

Giving one yourself: thank them, blame the situation, leave the door open. 'Qué bueno que me invitaste, fijate que ese domingo andamos donde la familia. Avisame para la otra.'

patterns.title: Qué harías vos — Would
patterns.text:
Add the imperfect ending to the whole infinitive. No stem changes, nothing to learn.

• hablaría, comería, viviría
• haría, diría, podría, tendría (short stems)

What it is for here:
• ¿Qué harías vos? — asking advice
• Yo diría que sí — softening an opinion
• ¿Me podría ayudar? — the polite ask

'Podría' and 'sería' turn a request into a question, which is most of what politeness is in this country.

patterns.title: Ojalá — Wishing, and the Subjunctive
patterns.text:
'Ojalá' always takes the subjunctive.

• Ojalá que venga — I hope he comes
• Ojalá no llueva
• Ojalá pueda ir

The present subjunctive swaps the vowel: -ar verbs take -e, -er/-ir verbs take -a.
• hable, coma, viva

Same after 'que' when you want somebody else to do something:
• Quiero que vengas
• Dice que lo hagas

And in the goodbyes: 'Que le vaya bien', 'Que descanse'.

patterns.title: Aquí se hace así — The Se That Has No Doer
patterns.text:
'Se' plus the verb says a thing is done, without saying who does it.

• Aquí se hace así — this is how it is done here
• Eso no se dice — you do not say that
• Se come con la mano

It is everywhere in kitchens, where nobody says 'I put in':
• Se le pone la sal y se deja media hora

It is also how a rule gets stated without anybody being told off. 'Eso no se hace' is a correction with no finger pointed.

patterns.title: Hace dos años — How Long
patterns.text:
'Hace' plus a length of time means AGO.

• Llegué hace dos años
• Hace rato — a while back

With 'que' plus the present, it means how long something HAS been going on:
• Hace dos años que vivo aquí — I've lived here two years
• ¿Cuánto hace que lo conocés?

Also common: 'Ya van tres años' — that's three years now. 'Llevo cinco años aquí' — I've been here five years.

patterns.title: Lo que, lo de — The Thing About
patterns.text:
'Lo' turns anything into an abstract 'the thing'.

• lo que dijo — what he said
• lo del banco — the bank business
• lo de ayer — that thing yesterday
• lo bueno es que — the good thing is

'Lo de' is how delicate matters get named without naming them. 'Lo de Chino' can mean his lost job, his father, or the money, and everybody in the room knows which.

patterns.title: Reclamar — Complaining So It Works
patterns.text:
A complaint that starts as an accusation gets you nowhere. The person at the window did not do it.

The shape that works:
• Fíjese que este recibo me llegó muy alto (a problem, not a fault)
• Aquí traigo el anterior (evidence)
• ¿Y con quién tengo que hablar? (the next door)
• Muchas gracias por la ayuda (they will remember)

Never 'ustedes me cobraron de más'. Ustedes makes them the company and they will defend it.

patterns.title: Mi amor — What People Actually Call Each Other
patterns.text:
Endearments here are not reserved for a partner.

• mi amor, mi vida, mi cielo, corazón — a shop lady says these to a stranger
• mijo / mija — from mi hijo, said to anybody younger
• papito, mamita — warm, everyday, not strange

In the fritanga they mean nothing and everything. Between two people they mean what you would expect.

Not using them at all is what marks you out, not using them wrongly.

patterns.title: Te quiero and Te amo Are Not the Same Size
patterns.text:
• Te quiero — warm, real, and usable long before 'te amo'. Said to family, to close friends, to a partner.
• Te amo — heavier, later, and said far less often than films suggest.

Saying 'te amo' too early sounds like a telenovela. Saying 'te quiero' to a friend is completely normal.

Also: 'me caés bien' is liking a person, which is a different verb again — and it is what you say about somebody you have just met.

patterns.title: Siempre and Nunca — The Words That Start Fights
patterns.text:
An argument here rarely breaks over the subject. It breaks over these two words.

• 'No me avisaste' — about one occasion, repairable
• 'Vos nunca me avisás' — about a whole character, not repairable

Same with 'siempre': 'siempre es tu mamá primero' turns one December into every December.

Keep it to the thing that happened. 'Uno' does the same job when you need distance: 'uno se queda esperando' says it without accusing anybody.

patterns.title: Perdón, disculpe, perdoname
patterns.text:
• Perdón — the small one. Bumping somebody, interrupting.
• Disculpe — formal, and it also opens a question to a stranger: 'Disculpe, ¿dónde está el baño?'
• Perdoname / discúlpeme — a real apology to a person.

For something that matters: say it short, in person, early. A long apology turns into an excuse.

Never 'perdón SI te ofendí'. The 'si' says it might not have happened. It did.

And nobody here says 'te perdono'. They offer you coffee.

patterns.title: Usted Inside a Family
patterns.text:
Usted between people who love each other is not coldness.

• A daughter calls her mother usted; the mother calls her vos
• In the countryside a husband and wife of fifty years use usted with each other
• A yerno uses usted with the suegra for years, sometimes forever

It is respect that has been running so long it became affection.

Do not switch to vos with a suegra to seem closer. Wait to be dropped, and it may never happen, and that is fine.

patterns.title: Mi pésame — What to Say When Somebody Dies
patterns.text:
There is a fixed thing to say and you are not expected to improvise.

• Mi pésame
• Lo siento mucho
• Que en paz descanse
• Lo acompaño en su sentimiento (formal)

Then you stop talking. The whole job is being there.

You arrive AT ONCE — within the hour, not when convenient. Everything else in this country runs late; this does not.

Take something for the coffee. Nine nights of it is a real cost to that house.

patterns.title: Tuani, maje, chocho — and Who Can Say Them
patterns.text:
• tuani — good, nice. Safe with almost anybody now.
• deacachimba — the same but much stronger. Friends only.
• chocho — an exclamation. Surprise, price, heat, anything.
• maje — mate, but also idiot. Tone decides.
• chavalo/a — kid, young person.

THE RULE IS NOT THE WORD, IT IS WHO HEARS IT. Deacachimba among teenagers is nothing. Out of a married man's mouth in front of a woman of eighty it is a different word entirely.

Ask before you use a new one: who says it, and in front of whom.

patterns.title: Un montón, un cachimbo, ni de vara
patterns.text:
Exaggerating here is not lying. A story is expected to grow, and correcting the size is bad manners.

• un montón de — loads of (mild, safe anywhere)
• un cachimbo de — loads of (strong, friends only)
• ni de vara — not a chance

'Ni de vara' is stronger than no. A no can be argued with; ni de vara ends it and gets a laugh.

Don Beto's fish has been growing for twenty years. Nobody has ever asked him how big it really was.

patterns.title: Pues, va, fijate, ideay
patterns.text:
Half of a Nicaraguan conversation is not words. Take them out and people will ask what is wrong with you.

• pues — closes a sentence. Dale pues, va pues, ya pues
• va — a tiny question at the end, asking for agreement
• fijate — something that matters is coming
• imaginate — something unbelievable is coming
• ideay — hello, or a complaint. Tone decides

Silence gets covered too. Three seconds of nothing is uncomfortable and somebody will put an 'aha' or an 'mmm' into it.

Speaking without them sounds like a doctor reading from a paper.

patterns.title: Dicen que — Saying It Without Owning It
patterns.text:
Gossip is how the barrio finds out about a wake, a birth, or a job. It is the newspaper, and it has its own grammar.

• Dicen que...
• Me contaron que...
• Oí decir que...
• Por ahí me dijeron

None of these ever names a source. That is the point: the teller is not responsible for it.

The rule that follows: anything you tell one mouth belongs to the barrio. There are no closed mouths, only slower ones.

patterns.title: Hora nica — When a Time Is Not a Time
patterns.text:
An invitation for twelve means about half past one. Nobody is lying and nobody is late.

What the phrases mean:
• Ya voy — has not got up
• Ya casi — an hour away
• Voy en camino — is in the shower
• Estoy a la vuelta — twenty minutes

Which times ARE real: anything with paperwork behind it. Work, the bus, mass, a hospital appointment.

And one more that is always kept: a velorio. Everything else runs late; nobody arrives late to grief.

patterns.title: The Goodbye Takes Forty Minutes
patterns.text:
Leaving a house has four stages and skipping them is rude.

1. Say 'bueno' from the chair. Ten more minutes of talking.
2. Stand up. Do not walk. Another ten.
3. The portón. Twenty minutes, and this is where the real thing gets said — it is the only place with no witnesses.
4. They walk you a block.

If you want to leave at nine, say 'bueno' at eight.

They insist you stay. Once is courtesy, twice is courtesy, three times means stay. Never say adiós — that is for the dead and for people leaving the country. Say nos vemos, cuidate.

patterns.title: Depende — Why Nobody Gives You a Straight Answer
patterns.text:
A definite answer commits the speaker, and somebody who commits can end up looking bad. Looking bad is worse here than not knowing.

So the answer hedges:
• Depende — the strongest one
• Más o menos — works for absolutely anything
• Puede ser — sounds like yes, is a polite doubt
• Digamos que — for the educated version
• Fíjese que — an excuse is already attached

Speaking with certainty about everything reads as thinking a lot of yourself, which is the worst fault there is. Even the doctor says 'puede ser'.

To get a real answer, do not push for yes or no. Ask what it depends on, then ask what he thinks is more likely.

patterns.title: Con todo respeto — Disagreeing Upwards
patterns.text:
There are two hierarchies: the one on the paperwork, and the real one, which runs on age and years served.

Correcting somebody above you in the real one has a shape:
1. Ask leave first — 'Con todo respeto', 'Si me permite'
2. Put the fault on yourself — 'Yo debo estar equivocado, pero...'
3. Let HIM find it and fix it. Do not fix it for him.

Contradicting an older man is not forbidden. Contradicting him IN FRONT OF PEOPLE is. In private you can say almost anything.

Afterwards nobody mentions it again. That silence is the point of the whole manoeuvre.

patterns.title: Es que fíjese — The Reason Repairs the Relationship
patterns.text:
A delay with no reason is disrespect. A delay with a reason is only a delay. The reason does not fix the job, it fixes the relationship - and the relationship is what is being looked after.

The shape, every time:
• Es que... (a reason is coming, not a no)
• fíjese / fijate (usted or vos, pick correctly)
• the reason, which happened TO him and is never his fault
• a NEW DATE - and that date is the real promise

He will talk first, before you can complain. That is deliberate: a complaint that never gets made is a wound that never happens.

Not complaining the first time buys you priority the next time.

patterns.title: Quería preguntarle — The Past Tense as Politeness
patterns.text:
Wanting something in the present is blunt. Put it in the past and it softens, even though you want it right now.

• Quiero preguntarle → Quería preguntarle
• Vengo a pedirle → Venía a ver si podía pedirle
• Estaba pensando que tal vez usted podría... (three softeners in one sentence)

And the phrase that warns something heavy is coming: 'No hallaba cómo decirle.'

Bad news and big requests are never dropped on somebody. You talk about the heat and the gas for fifteen minutes first. That is not padding, it is the preparation.

patterns.title: Uno — Saying I Without Saying I
patterns.text:
'Uno' means one, and it means me.

• Uno se queda pensando en esas cosas
• A uno le duele por años y no lo dice

Both of those are about the speaker, and everybody knows it. The distance is what makes them sayable at all.

Watch when people switch. Happy things get 'yo': 'yo compré la moto'. Hard things get 'uno'. Joy is signed; pain is left anonymous.

It also carries a complaint nobody can answer: 'Uno hace las cosas y nadie se lo agradece.' No one was accused, so no one can argue.

The one place it does not belong is with the person closest to you. Being able to say 'yo' with no distance in front of it is what confianza actually is.

patterns.title: The Hint, and How It Is Answered
patterns.text:
A straight request obliges the other person to say yes or no, and a no leaves them both looking bad. So the request is not made.

HOW IT IS THROWN: state a problem, ask for nothing, change the subject immediately. 'Y ahí el techo goteando desde mayo.' Then talk about something else.

It is thrown ONCE. Repeating it turns it into a complaint.

HOW IT IS ANSWERED: you offer, as though it were your own idea. Never '¿quiere que se lo arregle?' - that says out loud that she asked. Say 'el domingo ando por allá, llevo la escalera'.

She will refuse once. That refusal is part of it. Insist once and it is agreed. And nobody says thank you afterwards - lunch is the thank you.

patterns.title: Ni modo — What It Is Actually For
patterns.text:
It looks like giving up. It is not the first answer, it is the twelfth.

• Ni modo
• Qué se le va a hacer
• Así es la vida
• Es lo que hay
• Dios sabe lo que hace

The man who says it has already complained, already lost and already put up with it. Somebody went to the alcaldía eleven times about that drain.

What it does: it gets the anger out of the body in two words, so it does not come out at the wife and the children instead. It is a way of holding out without breaking.

And it is not the same as doing nothing. You can say ni modo tonight and still go to the alcaldía on Monday.

patterns.title: Hablando de eso — Steering Without Pushing
patterns.text:
You do not raise a difficult subject. You arrive at it on foot.

• Hablando de eso — hooks any subject to any other. Nobody ever checks whether you really were talking about that
• Por cierto — sounds like you just remembered
• Volviendo a lo de antes — reopens something dropped
• Aprovechando que estamos aquí — the softest way into a request

Put one or two subjects in between. You do not jump from the baseball to the money.

The rule underneath: a conversation is LED, not pushed. Same as the dance floor - you signal what is coming with your hand, and the other person arrives with you without feeling moved.

patterns.title: Ya en serio — The Moment the Joking Stops
patterns.text:
An evening of teasing can turn in one word, usually around eleven.

The signals:
• Ya en serio
• La verdad es que...
• Te voy a decir una cosa
• Somebody stops laughing before the others - the hardest one to see and the most important

Answering the new tone in the old one is the worst mistake available. It is the same as laughing at a wake.

In this register nobody interrupts, where in the joking one everybody does. Two different sets of rules at the same table.

Afterwards it is never mentioned again in the group. If you want to ask, ask alone, at the door.

patterns.title: Como decía mi abuela — Quoting the Dead
patterns.text:
A living person can be argued with. A dead grandmother cannot.

• Como decía mi abuela...
• Mi papá siempre dijo que...

It ends the argument, and not because it is a good point. Contradicting somebody's dead mother is a rudeness nobody will commit.

A refrán does the same job without a name attached, which is why quoting one also closes a subject.

Whether she really said it is the one question that is never asked. Very often the quote finishes an idea the dead person held all their life and never put into a sentence. That is not misquoting - here it counts as finishing it for them.

lessons.title: El calor
lessons.desc: You land, and the heat decides everything

sn.s: Llego a Nicaragua.
sn.e: I arrive in Nicaragua.

sn.s: El avión baja despacio.
sn.e: The plane comes down slowly.

sn.s: Por la ventana del avión veo agua.
sn.e: Through the window of the plane I see water.

sn.s: Es un lago muy grande.
sn.e: It is a very big lake.

sn.s: El avión toca la tierra.
sn.e: The plane touches the ground.

sn.s: Ya estoy en Managua.
sn.e: I am in Managua now.

sn.s: Abren la puerta del avión.
sn.e: They open the door of the plane.

sn.s: Y entonces llega el calor.
sn.e: And then the heat arrives.

sn.s: No es un calor normal.
sn.e: It is not a normal heat.

sn.s: Es un calor que pesa.
sn.e: It is a heat that weighs on you.

sn.s: El calor entra en el avión.
sn.e: The heat comes into the plane.

sn.s: La gente no dice nada.
sn.e: The people say nothing.

sn.s: Para ellos el calor es normal.
sn.e: For them the heat is normal.

sn.s: Bajo del avión con mi maleta.
sn.e: I get off the plane with my suitcase.

sn.s: El aeropuerto es pequeño.
sn.e: The airport is small.

sn.s: El aeropuerto se llama Augusto C. Sandino.
sn.e: The airport is called Augusto C. Sandino.

sn.s: Adentro del aeropuerto también hace calor.
sn.e: Inside the airport it is hot too.

sn.s: Un señor revisa mi pasaporte.
sn.e: A man checks my passport.

sn.s: "Buenas", dice el señor.
sn.e: "Buenas," the man says.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: Es mi primera palabra en Nicaragua.
sn.e: It is my first word in Nicaragua.

sn.s: El señor no pregunta nada más.
sn.e: The man does not ask anything else.

sn.s: Salgo del aeropuerto con mi maleta.
sn.e: I leave the airport with my suitcase.

sn.s: Afuera del aeropuerto hay mucha gente.
sn.e: Outside the airport there are a lot of people.

sn.s: Afuera el calor es peor.
sn.e: Outside the heat is worse.

sn.s: Hay muchos taxis en la calle.
sn.e: There are many taxis in the street.

sn.s: Hay muchos señores esperando.
sn.e: There are many men waiting.

sn.s: "¡Taxi, taxi!", dicen los señores.
sn.e: "Taxi, taxi!" the men say.

sn.s: Un señor se acerca.
sn.e: One man comes over.

sn.s: "Buenas, ¿para dónde va?", me dice.
sn.e: "Buenas, where are you going?" he says to me.

sn.s: No entiendo bien.
sn.e: I do not understand properly.

sn.s: El señor habla muy rápido.
sn.e: The man talks very fast.

sn.s: "¿Para dónde va?", dice otra vez.
sn.e: "Where are you going?" he says again.

sn.s: Ahora habla despacio.
sn.e: Now he talks slowly.

sn.s: Le enseño un papel.
sn.e: I show him a piece of paper.

sn.s: En el papel está la dirección.
sn.e: The address is on the paper.

sn.s: El señor lee el papel.
sn.e: The man reads the paper.

sn.s: "Ah, sí. Yo lo llevo."
sn.e: "Ah, yes. I'll take you."

sn.s: "¿Cuánto?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "How much?" I ask.

sn.s: Es la segunda palabra que uso aquí.
sn.e: It is the second word I use here.

sn.s: El señor dice un número.
sn.e: The man says a number.

sn.s: No entiendo el número.
sn.e: I do not understand the number.

sn.s: Digo que sí.
sn.e: I say yes.

sn.s: Después voy a saber que pagué mucho.
sn.e: Later I am going to find out that I paid a lot.

sn.s: Mucho, mucho más de lo normal.
sn.e: A lot, a lot more than normal.

sn.s: Pero eso es después.
sn.e: But that comes later.

sn.s: Subo al taxi.
sn.e: I get into the taxi.

sn.s: El taxi no tiene aire.
sn.e: The taxi has no air conditioning.

sn.s: Las ventanas del taxi están abiertas.
sn.e: The windows of the taxi are open.

sn.s: El calor entra por las ventanas.
sn.e: The heat comes in through the windows.

sn.s: El señor maneja y habla.
sn.e: The man drives and talks.

sn.s: Habla del calor.
sn.e: He talks about the heat.

sn.s: "Hace calor, ¿verdad?", me dice.
sn.e: "It's hot, isn't it?" he says to me.

sn.s: "Sí", digo yo. "Mucho calor."
sn.e: "Yes," I say. "Very hot."

sn.s: El señor se ríe.
sn.e: The man laughs.

sn.s: "Esto no es nada", dice.
sn.e: "This is nothing," he says.

sn.s: "En abril sí hace calor."
sn.e: "In April it really is hot."

sn.s: Es enero.
sn.e: It is January.

sn.s: Pienso en abril y tengo miedo.
sn.e: I think about April and I am afraid.

sn.s: Pasamos por la ciudad.
sn.e: We drive through the city.

sn.s: Veo casas de muchos colores.
sn.e: I see houses in many colours.

sn.s: Veo mucha gente en la calle.
sn.e: I see a lot of people in the street.

sn.s: Nadie camina rápido.
sn.e: Nobody walks fast.

sn.s: Ahora entiendo por qué.
sn.e: Now I understand why.

sn.s: Con este calor nadie camina rápido.
sn.e: In this heat nobody walks fast.

sn.s: El taxi para en una calle pequeña.
sn.e: The taxi stops in a small street.

sn.s: "Aquí es", dice el señor.
sn.e: "This is it," the man says.

sn.s: Le pago.
sn.e: I pay him.

sn.s: "Gracias", digo yo.
sn.e: "Thank you," I say.

sn.s: Es mi tercera palabra.
sn.e: It is my third word.

sn.s: En Nicaragua se dice gracias por todo.
sn.e: In Nicaragua you say thank you for everything.

sn.s: "Gracias a usted", dice el señor.
sn.e: "Thank *you*," the man says.

sn.s: Y se va.
sn.e: And he leaves.

sn.s: Estoy solo en la calle.
sn.e: I am alone in the street.

sn.s: Son las dos de la tarde.
sn.e: It is two in the afternoon.

sn.s: Hace mucho calor.
sn.e: It is very hot.

sn.s: No hay nadie en la calle.
sn.e: There is nobody in the street.

sn.s: Una señora sale de una casa.
sn.e: A woman comes out of a house.

sn.s: La señora me ve.
sn.e: The woman sees me.

sn.s: "Buenas", dice ella.
sn.e: "Buenas," she says.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: La señora entra otra vez en la casa.
sn.e: The woman goes back into the house.

sn.s: Sale con un vaso de agua.
sn.e: She comes out with a glass of water.

sn.s: "Tome", me dice. "Hace calor."
sn.e: "Here you go," she says to me. "It's hot."

sn.s: Tomo el vaso de agua.
sn.e: I take the glass of water.

sn.s: El agua está fría.
sn.e: The water is cold.

sn.s: Tomo toda el agua.
sn.e: I drink all the water.

sn.s: "Gracias", digo yo.
sn.e: "Thank you," I say.

sn.s: "De nada", dice la señora.
sn.e: "You're welcome," the woman says.

sn.s: Le digo gracias otra vez.
sn.e: I say thank you to her again.

sn.s: No sé cómo se llama la señora.
sn.e: I do not know the woman's name.

sn.s: Ella no sabe cómo me llamo yo.
sn.e: She does not know mine.

sn.s: Pero me da un vaso de agua.
sn.e: But she gives me a glass of water.

sn.s: Aquí hace mucho calor.
sn.e: Here it is very hot.

sn.s: Y aquí la gente da agua.
sn.e: And here people give you water.

sn.s: Las dos cosas son ciertas.
sn.e: Both things are true.

sn.s: Ese es mi primer día en Nicaragua.
sn.e: That is my first day in Nicaragua.

lessons.title: Buenas
lessons.desc: One word does the work of ten

sn.s: Es mi segundo día en Nicaragua.
sn.e: It is my second day in Nicaragua.

sn.s: Salgo de la casa por la mañana.
sn.e: I leave the house in the morning.

sn.s: Hace calor otra vez.
sn.e: It is hot again.

sn.s: Camino por la calle.
sn.e: I walk down the street.

sn.s: En la calle hay mucha gente.
sn.e: There are a lot of people in the street.

sn.s: Un señor está en la puerta de su casa.
sn.e: A man is in the doorway of his house.

sn.s: El señor me ve.
sn.e: The man sees me.

sn.s: "Buenas", me dice.
sn.e: "Buenas," he says to me.

sn.s: Yo no digo nada.
sn.e: I say nothing.

sn.s: Camino más rápido.
sn.e: I walk faster.

sn.s: Una señora barre la puerta de su casa.
sn.e: A woman sweeps her doorway.

sn.s: "Buenas", me dice la señora.
sn.e: "Buenas," the woman says to me.

sn.s: Yo no digo nada otra vez.
sn.e: Again I say nothing.

sn.s: Dos chavalos están en la calle.
sn.e: Two kids are in the street.

sn.s: "Buenas", dicen los chavalos.
sn.e: "Buenas," the kids say.

sn.s: Yo sigo caminando.
sn.e: I keep walking.

sn.s: Siento algo raro.
sn.e: I feel something strange.

sn.s: La gente me mira.
sn.e: The people look at me.

sn.s: No sé por qué.
sn.e: I do not know why.

sn.s: Un chavalo camina conmigo.
sn.e: A kid walks along with me.

sn.s: "¿Por qué no saluda?", me pregunta.
sn.e: "Why don't you say hello?" he asks me.

sn.s: "¿Saludar?", digo yo.
sn.e: "Say hello?" I say.

sn.s: "Sí. Aquí uno saluda."
sn.e: "Yes. Here you say hello."

sn.s: "¿A quién?", pregunto.
sn.e: "To who?" I ask.

sn.s: "A todos", dice el chavalo.
sn.e: "To everyone," the kid says.

sn.s: "¿A toda la gente de la calle?"
sn.e: "To all the people in the street?"

sn.s: "A toda la gente", dice.
sn.e: "To everyone," he says.

sn.s: Roberto me explica cómo saludar.
sn.e: Roberto explains to me how to say hello.

sn.s: Uno saluda al vecino de al lado.
sn.e: You greet the neighbour next door.

sn.s: Uno saluda al vecino de enfrente.
sn.e: You greet the neighbour opposite.

sn.s: Uno saluda hasta al que no conoce.
sn.e: You even greet the one you do not know.

sn.s: "Saludar no cuesta nada", dice el chavalo.
sn.e: "Saying hello costs nothing," the kid says.

sn.s: Otro chavalo pasa y me saluda.
sn.e: Another kid goes past and greets me.

sn.s: Los chavalos de esta calle saludan a todos.
sn.e: The kids on this street greet everybody.

sn.s: El chavalo se llama Roberto.
sn.e: The kid is called Roberto.

sn.s: Roberto tiene doce años.
sn.e: Roberto is twelve years old.

sn.s: Roberto vive en la casa de al lado.
sn.e: Roberto lives in the house next door.

sn.s: Entonces Roberto es mi vecino.
sn.e: So Roberto is my neighbour.

sn.s: "Yo soy tu vecino", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "I'm your neighbour," Roberto says.

sn.s: "Y mi mamá es tu vecina."
sn.e: "And my mum is your neighbour too."

sn.s: Un vecino es el que vive al lado.
sn.e: A neighbour is the one who lives next door.

sn.s: Aquí uno conoce a todos sus vecinos.
sn.e: Here you know all your neighbours.

sn.s: Roberto me enseña.
sn.e: Roberto teaches me.

sn.s: "En la mañana se dice buenos días."
sn.e: "In the morning you say buenos días."

sn.s: "En la tarde se dice buenas tardes."
sn.e: "In the afternoon you say buenas tardes."

sn.s: "En la noche se dice buenas noches."
sn.e: "At night you say buenas noches."

sn.s: "Pero uno casi siempre dice buenas."
sn.e: "But you nearly always just say buenas."

sn.s: "¿Buenas y nada más?", pregunto.
sn.e: "Just buenas and nothing else?" I ask.

sn.s: "Buenas y nada más", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Buenas and nothing else," Roberto says.

sn.s: "Buenas sirve en la mañana."
sn.e: "Buenas works in the morning."

sn.s: "Buenas sirve en la tarde."
sn.e: "Buenas works in the afternoon."

sn.s: "Y buenas sirve en la noche."
sn.e: "And buenas works at night."

sn.s: Volvemos por la misma calle.
sn.e: We go back down the same street.

sn.s: Los dos chavalos están en la puerta.
sn.e: The two kids are in the doorway.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: "Buenas", dicen ellos.
sn.e: "Buenas," they say.

sn.s: La señora sigue en la puerta de su casa.
sn.e: The woman is still in her doorway.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: La señora sonríe.
sn.e: The woman smiles.

sn.s: "Buenas tardes, joven", me dice.
sn.e: "Good afternoon, young man," she says to me.

sn.s: El señor está en su puerta.
sn.e: The man is in his doorway.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: "Buenas", dice el señor.
sn.e: "Buenas," the man says.

sn.s: Y ahora la calle es otra calle.
sn.e: And now the street is a different street.

sn.s: La misma gente, la misma calle.
sn.e: The same people, the same street.

sn.s: Pero ahora la gente me habla.
sn.e: But now the people talk to me.

sn.s: Roberto me lleva a su casa.
sn.e: Roberto takes me to his house.

sn.s: En la puerta está su mamá.
sn.e: His mum is in the doorway.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: "Buenas", dice ella. "¿Cómo se llama usted?"
sn.e: "Buenas," she says. "What's your name?"

sn.s: Le digo mi nombre.
sn.e: I tell her my name.

sn.s: Ella dice su nombre: Carmen.
sn.e: She says her name: Carmen.

sn.s: "Doña Carmen", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Doña Carmen," Roberto says.

sn.s: "Aquí a las señoras se les dice doña."
sn.e: "Here you call women doña."

sn.s: "Y a los señores se les dice don."
sn.e: "And you call men don."

sn.s: Doña Carmen me da un vaso de agua.
sn.e: Doña Carmen gives me a glass of water.

sn.s: "Gracias, doña Carmen", digo yo.
sn.e: "Thank you, doña Carmen," I say.

sn.s: En la noche pienso en la calle.
sn.e: At night I think about the street.

sn.s: Ayer la gente no me habló.
sn.e: Yesterday the people did not talk to me.

sn.s: Hoy la gente me habló.
sn.e: Today the people talked to me.

sn.s: Y sólo dije una palabra.
sn.e: And I only said one word.

sn.s: Buenas.
sn.e: Buenas.

lessons.title: Córdobas
lessons.desc: Money that is not yours yet

sn.s: Necesito comprar agua.
sn.e: I need to buy water.

sn.s: Aquí uno compra el agua en bolsa o en botella.
sn.e: Here you buy water in a bag or a bottle.

sn.s: Voy a comprar agua y algo de comer.
sn.e: I am going to buy water and something to eat.

sn.s: Hace calor y no tengo agua en el cuarto.
sn.e: It is hot and I have no water in my room.

sn.s: Doña Carmen me dice dónde comprar.
sn.e: Doña Carmen tells me where to buy it.

sn.s: "En la esquina", dice ella.
sn.e: "On the corner," she says.

sn.s: Voy a la esquina de la calle.
sn.e: I go to the corner of the street.

sn.s: Hay una señora con una mesa.
sn.e: There is a woman with a table.

sn.s: En la mesa hay agua, pan y fruta.
sn.e: On the table there is water, bread and fruit.

sn.s: "Buenas", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas," I say.

sn.s: "Buenas", dice la señora.
sn.e: "Buenas," the woman says.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto cuesta el agua?", pregunto.
sn.e: "How much does the water cost?" I ask.

sn.s: "Quince", dice la señora.
sn.e: "Fifteen," the woman says.

sn.s: "¿Quince qué?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "Fifteen what?" I ask.

sn.s: La señora se ríe.
sn.e: The woman laughs.

sn.s: "Quince pesos, joven."
sn.e: "Fifteen pesos, young man."

sn.s: Yo no entiendo.
sn.e: I do not understand.

sn.s: Aquí la plata se llama córdoba.
sn.e: Here the money is called the córdoba.

sn.s: Pero la gente dice pesos.
sn.e: But people say pesos.

sn.s: Córdoba en el papel, peso en la boca.
sn.e: Córdoba on the paper, peso in the mouth.

sn.s: Le doy un billete de cien córdobas.
sn.e: I give her a hundred-córdoba note.

sn.s: La señora me da el vuelto.
sn.e: The woman gives me my change.

sn.s: Cuento el vuelto despacio.
sn.e: I count the change slowly.

sn.s: Ochenta y cinco córdobas.
sn.e: Eighty-five córdobas.

sn.s: Está bien.
sn.e: That is right.

sn.s: "Gracias", digo yo.
sn.e: "Thank you," I say.

sn.s: Después compro pan.
sn.e: Then I buy bread.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto cuesta el pan?", pregunto.
sn.e: "How much does the bread cost?" I ask.

sn.s: "Diez pesos", dice la señora.
sn.e: "Ten pesos," the woman says.

sn.s: Comprar pan cuesta poco.
sn.e: Buying bread costs little.

sn.s: Comprar agua cuesta un poco más.
sn.e: Buying water costs a little more.

sn.s: Todo lo que compro hoy es barato.
sn.e: Everything I buy today is cheap.

sn.s: Yo pago con un billete grande.
sn.e: I pay with a big note.

sn.s: La señora dice que no es caro.
sn.e: The woman says it is not expensive.

sn.s: Aquí las cosas cuestan poco.
sn.e: Here things cost little.

sn.s: Un vaso de agua no cuesta nada.
sn.e: A glass of water costs nothing.

sn.s: Pero un taxi puede costar mucho.
sn.e: But a taxi can cost a lot.

sn.s: Pero uno tiene que preguntar cuánto cuesta.
sn.e: But you have to ask how much it costs.

sn.s: Y después uno paga.
sn.e: And then you pay.

sn.s: Nunca se paga antes de preguntar.
sn.e: You never pay before asking.

sn.s: Eso es barato y eso es caro.
sn.e: That is cheap and that is expensive.

sn.s: Diez córdobas por el pan.
sn.e: Ten córdobas for the bread.

sn.s: Eso es barato.
sn.e: That is cheap.

sn.s: Todo aquí es barato para mí.
sn.e: Everything here is cheap for me.

sn.s: Pero no es barato para la gente de aquí.
sn.e: But it is not cheap for the people here.

sn.s: Eso lo entiendo después.
sn.e: I understand that later.

sn.s: Aquí hay que saber lo que cuesta cada cosa.
sn.e: Here you have to know what each thing costs.

sn.s: En la casa le enseño el pan a Roberto.
sn.e: At the house I show Roberto the bread.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto pagaste?", pregunta Roberto.
sn.e: "How much did you pay?" Roberto asks.

sn.s: "Diez pesos", digo yo.
sn.e: "Ten pesos," I say.

sn.s: "Está bien", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "That is right," Roberto says.

sn.s: "¿Y el agua?", pregunta.
sn.e: "And the water?" he asks.

sn.s: "Quince pesos."
sn.e: "Fifteen pesos."

sn.s: "También está bien."
sn.e: "That is right too."

sn.s: Entonces Roberto me pregunta por el taxi.
sn.e: Then Roberto asks me about the taxi.

sn.s: "¿Cuánto pagaste del aeropuerto?"
sn.e: "How much did you pay from the airport?"

sn.s: No me acuerdo bien del número.
sn.e: I do not remember the number properly.

sn.s: Le enseño lo que tengo en la mano.
sn.e: I show him what I have in my hand.

sn.s: Roberto abre los ojos.
sn.e: Roberto's eyes open wide.

sn.s: "¡Ideay! Eso es muy caro."
sn.e: "Ideay! That is very expensive."

sn.s: "¿Caro?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "Expensive?" I ask.

sn.s: "Muy caro. Pagaste cuatro veces."
sn.e: "Very expensive. You paid four times over."

sn.s: Doña Carmen se ríe desde la cocina.
sn.e: Doña Carmen laughs from the kitchen.

sn.s: "Al chele siempre le cobran caro", dice.
sn.e: "They always charge the chele more," she says.

sn.s: Roberto me enseña una cosa.
sn.e: Roberto teaches me one thing.

sn.s: "Primero pregunte cuánto cuesta."
sn.e: "First ask how much it costs."

sn.s: "Siempre. Antes de subir al taxi."
sn.e: "Always. Before you get in the taxi."

sn.s: "Y si es muy caro, uno no paga."
sn.e: "And if it is too expensive, you do not pay."

sn.s: "¿Y qué digo?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "And what do I say?" I ask.

sn.s: "Diga: está muy caro."
sn.e: "Say: that's too expensive."

sn.s: "Está muy caro", digo yo.
sn.e: "That's too expensive," I say.

sn.s: "Así", dice Roberto. "Otra vez."
sn.e: "Like that," Roberto says. "Again."

sn.s: "Está muy caro."
sn.e: "That's too expensive."

sn.s: "Ahora sí", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Now you've got it," Roberto says.

sn.s: Esa noche cuento mi plata.
sn.e: That night I count my money.

sn.s: Tengo menos plata de la que pensaba.
sn.e: I have less money than I thought.

sn.s: El taxi me costó mucho.
sn.e: The taxi cost me a lot.

sn.s: El agua me costó quince pesos.
sn.e: The water cost me fifteen pesos.

sn.s: El pan me costó diez pesos.
sn.e: The bread cost me ten pesos.

sn.s: Y ahora sé cuánto cuestan las cosas.
sn.e: And now I know how much things cost.

sn.s: Mañana voy a preguntar primero.
sn.e: Tomorrow I am going to ask first.

lessons.title: Gallo pinto
lessons.desc: Breakfast, and there is no other option

sn.s: Es temprano.
sn.e: It is early.

sn.s: Todavía no hace calor.
sn.e: It is not hot yet.

sn.s: Doña Carmen está en la cocina.
sn.e: Doña Carmen is in the kitchen.

sn.s: De la cocina viene un olor rico.
sn.e: A good smell comes from the kitchen.

sn.s: "Buenas, doña Carmen", digo yo.
sn.e: "Buenas, doña Carmen," I say.

sn.s: "Buenas. Venga a comer", dice ella.
sn.e: "Buenas. Come and eat," she says.

sn.s: "No tengo hambre", digo yo.
sn.e: "I am not hungry," I say.

sn.s: Doña Carmen no me oye.
sn.e: Doña Carmen does not hear me.

sn.s: O no me quiere oír.
sn.e: Or does not want to hear me.

sn.s: Pone un plato en la mesa.
sn.e: She puts a plate on the table.

sn.s: En el plato hay arroz con frijoles.
sn.e: On the plate there is rice with beans.

sn.s: El arroz y los frijoles están juntos.
sn.e: The rice and the beans are together.

sn.s: "Esto se llama gallo pinto", dice.
sn.e: "This is called gallo pinto," she says.

sn.s: "¿Gallo pinto?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "Gallo pinto?" I ask.

sn.s: "Gallo pinto. Arroz y frijoles."
sn.e: "Gallo pinto. Rice and beans."

sn.s: El gallo pinto se come en la mañana.
sn.e: Gallo pinto is eaten in the morning.

sn.s: El gallo pinto lleva arroz y frijoles.
sn.e: Gallo pinto has rice and beans in it.

sn.s: Los frijoles son rojos y pequeños.
sn.e: The beans are red and small.

sn.s: Sin frijoles no hay gallo pinto.
sn.e: Without beans there is no gallo pinto.

sn.s: Doña Carmen cocina los frijoles en la cocina.
sn.e: Doña Carmen cooks the beans in the kitchen.

sn.s: En la cocina hay una olla grande de frijoles.
sn.e: In the kitchen there is a big pot of beans.

sn.s: En la cocina huele a café.
sn.e: The kitchen smells of coffee.

sn.s: El café se toma dulce aquí.
sn.e: Coffee is drunk sweet here.

sn.s: Tomo el café y como la tortilla.
sn.e: I drink the coffee and eat the tortilla.

sn.s: Comer en la mañana es importante.
sn.e: Eating in the morning is important.

sn.s: Aquí se come temprano.
sn.e: Here people eat early.

sn.s: Se come en la casa, no en la calle.
sn.e: People eat at home, not in the street.

sn.s: Comer solo aquí es raro.
sn.e: Eating alone is a strange thing here.

sn.s: Y se come mucho.
sn.e: And they eat a lot.

sn.s: Doña Carmen pone otro plato en la mesa.
sn.e: Doña Carmen puts another plate on the table.

sn.s: Ese plato es para Roberto.
sn.e: That plate is for Roberto.

sn.s: Al lado del gallo pinto hay una tortilla.
sn.e: Next to the gallo pinto there is a tortilla.

sn.s: La tortilla es gruesa y está caliente.
sn.e: The tortilla is thick and hot.

sn.s: También hay cuajada.
sn.e: There is cuajada too.

sn.s: La cuajada es blanca y salada.
sn.e: Cuajada is white and salty.

sn.s: Y hay café en un vaso.
sn.e: And there is coffee in a glass.

sn.s: El café está muy dulce.
sn.e: The coffee is very sweet.

sn.s: Doña Carmen se sienta.
sn.e: Doña Carmen sits down.

sn.s: Roberto también se sienta a comer.
sn.e: Roberto sits down to eat too.

sn.s: Roberto come rápido.
sn.e: Roberto eats fast.

sn.s: Doña Carmen come poco.
sn.e: Doña Carmen eats little.

sn.s: Ella prefiere ver comer a los demás.
sn.e: She would rather watch other people eat.

sn.s: Yo como despacio.
sn.e: I eat slowly.

sn.s: El gallo pinto está rico.
sn.e: The gallo pinto is good.

sn.s: Está muy rico.
sn.e: It is really good.

sn.s: "¿Le gusta?", pregunta doña Carmen.
sn.e: "Do you like it?" doña Carmen asks.

sn.s: "Me gusta mucho", digo yo.
sn.e: "I like it a lot," I say.

sn.s: "Está muy rico", digo.
sn.e: "It is very good," I say.

sn.s: Doña Carmen sonríe.
sn.e: Doña Carmen smiles.

sn.s: Pone más gallo pinto en mi plato.
sn.e: She puts more gallo pinto on my plate.

sn.s: "Doña Carmen, ya no", digo yo.
sn.e: "Doña Carmen, no more," I say.

sn.s: Ella pone más de todos modos.
sn.e: She puts more on anyway.

sn.s: "Coma", dice. "Está flaco."
sn.e: "Eat," she says. "You're thin."

sn.s: Roberto se ríe con la boca llena.
sn.e: Roberto laughs with his mouth full.

sn.s: "Mi mamá siempre dice eso", dice.
sn.e: "My mum always says that," he says.

sn.s: Como todo el gallo pinto.
sn.e: I eat all the gallo pinto.

sn.s: Como toda la tortilla.
sn.e: I eat all the tortilla.

sn.s: Tomo todo el café.
sn.e: I drink all the coffee.

sn.s: "¿Y mañana qué se come?", pregunto.
sn.e: "And what do we eat tomorrow?" I ask.

sn.s: Roberto me mira raro.
sn.e: Roberto gives me a strange look.

sn.s: "Gallo pinto", dice.
sn.e: "Gallo pinto," he says.

sn.s: "¿Y pasado mañana?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "And the day after?" I ask.

sn.s: "Gallo pinto", dice Roberto.
sn.e: "Gallo pinto," Roberto says.

sn.s: "¿Siempre gallo pinto?"
sn.e: "Always gallo pinto?"

sn.s: "Siempre", dice doña Carmen desde la cocina.
sn.e: "Always," doña Carmen says from the kitchen.

sn.s: "En la mañana, gallo pinto."
sn.e: "In the morning, gallo pinto."

sn.s: "Y a veces en la noche también."
sn.e: "And sometimes at night as well."

sn.s: Pienso que eso va a ser mucho arroz.
sn.e: I think that is going to be a lot of rice.

sn.s: Mucho arroz y muchos frijoles.
sn.e: A lot of rice and a lot of beans.

sn.s: Pero no digo nada.
sn.e: But I say nothing.

sn.s: El gallo pinto está rico.
sn.e: The gallo pinto is good.

sn.s: Doña Carmen me da otra tortilla.
sn.e: Doña Carmen gives me another tortilla.

sn.s: "Para el camino", dice.
sn.e: "For the road," she says.

sn.s: "Gracias, doña Carmen."
sn.e: "Thank you, doña Carmen."

sn.s: "De nada, mijo", dice ella.
sn.e: "You're welcome, mijo," she says.

sn.s: Es la primera vez que me dice mijo.
sn.e: It is the first time she calls me mijo.

sn.s: Roberto me explica en la calle.
sn.e: Roberto explains it to me in the street.

sn.s: "Mijo es como hijo", dice.
sn.e: "Mijo is like son," he says.

sn.s: "Mi mamá le dice mijo a todos."
sn.e: "My mum calls everyone mijo."

sn.s: Pero yo llegué hace tres días.
sn.e: But I arrived three days ago.

sn.s: Y ya como en su cocina.
sn.e: And I already eat in her kitchen.

sn.s: Y ya me dice mijo.
sn.e: And she already calls me mijo.

sn.s: Aquí la comida es una puerta.
sn.e: Here food is a door.

sn.s: Uno come y ya está adentro.
sn.e: You eat and you are inside.

lessons.title: El cuarto
lessons.desc: A room with a fan and no hot water

sn.s: Mi cuarto es pequeño.
sn.e: My room is small.

sn.s: En el cuarto hay una cama.
sn.e: In the room there is a bed.

sn.s: La cama es dura.
sn.e: The bed is hard.

sn.s: Al lado de la cama hay una silla.
sn.e: Next to the bed there is a chair.

sn.s: En la silla pongo mi ropa.
sn.e: I put my clothes on the chair.

sn.s: No hay más muebles en el cuarto.
sn.e: There is no other furniture in the room.

sn.s: El cuarto tiene una ventana.
sn.e: The room has a window.

sn.s: La ventana no tiene vidrio.
sn.e: The window has no glass.

sn.s: La ventana siempre está abierta.
sn.e: The window is always open.

sn.s: Por la ventana entra el calor.
sn.e: The heat comes in through the window.

sn.s: Por la ventana entran los ruidos de la calle.
sn.e: The noises of the street come in through the window.

sn.s: Por la ventana entra la música del vecino.
sn.e: The neighbour's music comes in through the window.

sn.s: Arriba de la cama hay un abanico.
sn.e: Above the bed there is a fan.

sn.s: El abanico da vueltas toda la noche.
sn.e: The fan turns all night.

sn.s: Sin el abanico no puedo dormir.
sn.e: Without the fan I cannot sleep.

sn.s: Con el abanico duermo bien.
sn.e: With the fan I sleep well.

sn.s: El abanico hace un ruido pequeño.
sn.e: The fan makes a small noise.

sn.s: Ese ruido ya me gusta.
sn.e: I have come to like that noise.

sn.s: El baño está afuera del cuarto.
sn.e: The bathroom is outside the room.

sn.s: En el baño no hay agua caliente.
sn.e: In the bathroom there is no hot water.

sn.s: En ninguna casa hay agua caliente.
sn.e: There is no hot water in any house.

sn.s: Roberto no entiende mi pregunta.
sn.e: Roberto does not understand my question.

sn.s: "¿Agua caliente? ¿Para qué?", dice.
sn.e: "Hot water? What for?" he says.

sn.s: "Hace calor todo el año."
sn.e: "It is hot all year."

sn.s: Tiene razón.
sn.e: He is right.

sn.s: En el baño hay una pila.
sn.e: In the bathroom there is a pila.

sn.s: La pila es de cemento.
sn.e: The pila is made of cement.

sn.s: La pila siempre está llena de agua.
sn.e: The pila is always full of water.

sn.s: Al lado de la pila hay un balde.
sn.e: Next to the pila there is a bucket.

sn.s: El balde es azul.
sn.e: The bucket is blue.

sn.s: El balde siempre está al lado de la pila.
sn.e: The bucket is always next to the pila.

sn.s: Sin balde uno no se puede bañar.
sn.e: Without a bucket you cannot wash.

sn.s: Uno no se mete en la pila.
sn.e: You do not get into the pila.

sn.s: Eso lo aprendo el primer día.
sn.e: I learn that on the first day.

sn.s: Uno saca el agua de la pila con el balde.
sn.e: You take the water out of the pila with the bucket.

sn.s: Después uno se echa el agua encima.
sn.e: Then you pour the water over yourself.

sn.s: El agua está fría.
sn.e: The water is cold.

sn.s: La primera vez es horrible.
sn.e: The first time it is horrible.

sn.s: La segunda vez es menos horrible.
sn.e: The second time it is less horrible.

sn.s: Después uno se acostumbra.
sn.e: Then you get used to it.

sn.s: Con este calor el agua fría es buena.
sn.e: In this heat cold water is good.

sn.s: Me baño con el balde en la mañana.
sn.e: I bathe with the bucket in the morning.

sn.s: Me baño con el balde en la noche.
sn.e: I bathe with the bucket at night.

sn.s: A veces me baño tres veces al día.
sn.e: Sometimes I bathe three times a day.

sn.s: El jabón está en una taza al lado de la pila.
sn.e: The soap is in a cup next to the pila.

sn.s: El jabón es azul y grande.
sn.e: The soap is blue and big.

sn.s: Ese jabón sirve para todo.
sn.e: That soap is for everything.

sn.s: Con ese jabón me baño.
sn.e: I bathe with that soap.

sn.s: Con ese jabón lavo mi ropa.
sn.e: I wash my clothes with that soap.

sn.s: Doña Carmen lava la ropa en la pila.
sn.e: Doña Carmen washes clothes in the pila.

sn.s: Lava la ropa todos los días.
sn.e: She washes clothes every day.

sn.s: La ropa se seca rápido con este calor.
sn.e: Clothes dry fast in this heat.

sn.s: Mi ropa se seca en dos horas.
sn.e: My clothes dry in two hours.

sn.s: La primera semana lavo mal mi ropa.
sn.e: The first week I wash my clothes badly.

sn.s: Doña Carmen me ve y se ríe.
sn.e: Doña Carmen sees me and laughs.

sn.s: "Así no, mijo", dice ella.
sn.e: "Not like that, mijo," she says.

sn.s: Me enseña cómo lavar la ropa en la pila.
sn.e: She shows me how to wash clothes in the pila.

sn.s: Ahora lavo mi ropa mejor.
sn.e: Now I wash my clothes better.

sn.s: En la noche cierro la puerta del cuarto.
sn.e: At night I close the door of the room.

sn.s: La ventana no la cierro.
sn.e: I do not close the window.

sn.s: No se puede cerrar la ventana con este calor.
sn.e: You cannot close the window in this heat.

sn.s: Prendo el abanico.
sn.e: I turn on the fan.

sn.s: Me acuesto en la cama dura.
sn.e: I lie down on the hard bed.

sn.s: Oigo la calle por la ventana.
sn.e: I hear the street through the window.

sn.s: Oigo el abanico arriba de la cama.
sn.e: I hear the fan above the bed.

sn.s: Y me duermo.
sn.e: And I fall asleep.

lessons.title: Se fue la luz
lessons.desc: The power goes and nobody reacts

sn.s: Son las ocho de la noche.
sn.e: It is eight at night.

sn.s: Estoy en mi cuarto.
sn.e: I am in my room.

sn.s: El abanico da vueltas.
sn.e: The fan is turning.

sn.s: La luz está prendida.
sn.e: The light is on.

sn.s: De repente todo se apaga.
sn.e: Suddenly everything goes off.

sn.s: Se apaga la luz.
sn.e: The light goes off.

sn.s: Se apaga el abanico.
sn.e: The fan goes off.

sn.s: Se apagan las luces de toda la calle.
sn.e: The lights of the whole street go off.

sn.s: Se apaga la música del vecino.
sn.e: The neighbour's music goes off.

sn.s: El cuarto queda oscuro.
sn.e: The room goes dark.

sn.s: Todo queda oscuro.
sn.e: Everything goes dark.

sn.s: No veo nada.
sn.e: I cannot see anything.

sn.s: Espero un momento.
sn.e: I wait a moment.

sn.s: La luz no vuelve.
sn.e: The light does not come back.

sn.s: Salgo del cuarto en lo oscuro.
sn.e: I leave the room in the dark.

sn.s: Toda la casa está oscura.
sn.e: The whole house is dark.

sn.s: Voy hacia la puerta.
sn.e: I go towards the door.

sn.s: Afuera también está oscuro.
sn.e: Outside it is dark too.

sn.s: Toda la calle está oscura.
sn.e: The whole street is dark.

sn.s: Todas las casas están oscuras.
sn.e: All the houses are dark.

sn.s: Pienso que es algo grave.
sn.e: I think it is something serious.

sn.s: Pero la gente está tranquila.
sn.e: But the people are calm.

sn.s: Doña Carmen sale con una vela.
sn.e: Doña Carmen comes out with a candle.

sn.s: Prende la vela con un fósforo.
sn.e: She lights the candle with a match.

sn.s: Pone la vela en la mesa.
sn.e: She puts the candle on the table.

sn.s: Prende otra vela para la cocina.
sn.e: She lights another candle for the kitchen.

sn.s: "¿Qué pasó?", pregunto yo.
sn.e: "What happened?" I ask.

sn.s: "Se fue la luz", dice doña Carmen.
sn.e: "The power went," doña Carmen says.

sn.s: Lo dice tranquila.
sn.e: She says it calmly.

sn.s: Como si no fuera nada.
sn.e: As if it were nothing.

sn.s: "¿Y cuándo vuelve?", pregunto.
sn.e: "And when does it come back?" I ask.

sn.s: "Vuelve cuando vuelve", dice ella.
sn.e: "It comes back when it comes back," she says.

sn.s: Roberto saca dos sillas a la calle.
sn.e: Roberto takes two chairs out to the street.

sn.s: Saca una silla para él.
sn.e: He takes out one chair for himself.

sn.s: Saca una silla para su mamá.
sn.e: He takes out one chair for his mum.

sn.s: Después saca una silla más.
sn.e: Then he takes out one more chair.

sn.s: "Esta silla es para vos", me dice.
sn.e: "This chair is for you," he says to me.

sn.s: Es la primera vez que me dice vos.
sn.e: It is the first time he says vos to me.

sn.s: Nos sentamos afuera en las sillas.
sn.e: We sit outside on the chairs.

sn.s: Los vecinos también sacan sillas.
sn.e: The neighbours take out chairs too.

sn.s: Toda la calle está afuera.
sn.e: The whole street is outside.

sn.s: Adentro de las casas hace más calor.
sn.e: It is hotter inside the houses.

sn.s: Sin abanico, adentro no se puede estar.
sn.e: Without a fan you cannot stay inside.

sn.s: Afuera corre un poco de aire.
sn.e: Outside there is a bit of a breeze.

sn.s: La gente habla de una casa a otra.
sn.e: People talk from one house to another.

sn.s: Nadie habla de la luz.
sn.e: Nobody talks about the power.

sn.s: Hablan de otras cosas.
sn.e: They talk about other things.

sn.s: Hablan del calor.
sn.e: They talk about the heat.

sn.s: Hablan de la comida.
sn.e: They talk about food.

sn.s: Un señor habla del béisbol.
sn.e: A man talks about baseball.

sn.s: Yo escucho y no entiendo todo.
sn.e: I listen and do not understand everything.

sn.s: Pero entiendo un poco.
sn.e: But I understand a little.

sn.s: Cada día entiendo un poco más.
sn.e: Every day I understand a little more.

sn.s: Las velas se ven en todas las puertas.
sn.e: Candles can be seen in every doorway.

sn.s: La calle está oscura y llena de gente.
sn.e: The street is dark and full of people.

sn.s: Pasan dos horas.
sn.e: Two hours go by.

sn.s: Nadie se queja.
sn.e: Nobody complains.

sn.s: Nadie llama a nadie.
sn.e: Nobody calls anyone.

sn.s: Sólo esperan.
sn.e: They just wait.

sn.s: Yo espero con ellos.
sn.e: I wait with them.

sn.s: De repente vuelve la luz.
sn.e: Suddenly the power comes back.

sn.s: Se prenden las luces de la calle.
sn.e: The street lights come on.

sn.s: Se prenden los abanicos.
sn.e: The fans come on.

sn.s: En las casas suena la música otra vez.
sn.e: Music starts again in the houses.

sn.s: La gente dice "¡ah!" y se ríe.
sn.e: People say "ah!" and laugh.

sn.s: Roberto apaga la vela con la mano.
sn.e: Roberto puts out the candle with his hand.

sn.s: Doña Carmen apaga la otra vela.
sn.e: Doña Carmen puts out the other candle.

sn.s: Los vecinos apagan sus velas también.
sn.e: The neighbours put out their candles too.

sn.s: Nadie apaga el abanico esa noche.
sn.e: Nobody turns off the fan that night.

sn.s: Uno no apaga el abanico nunca.
sn.e: You never turn off the fan.

sn.s: Todos meten las sillas a las casas.
sn.e: Everyone takes the chairs back into the houses.

sn.s: En cinco minutos la calle está vacía.
sn.e: In five minutes the street is empty.

sn.s: Vuelvo a mi cuarto.
sn.e: I go back to my room.

sn.s: Prendo el abanico otra vez.
sn.e: I turn the fan on again.

sn.s: Pienso en las dos horas afuera.
